title: Japanese milk bread
skill: A tangzhong for a soft crumb

move.title: A cooked paste for a cloud-soft loaf
move.body: Japanese milk bread (shokupan) is famous for a crumb so soft it pulls apart in feathery strands, and it stays fresh for days. The secret is tangzhong: a little flour cooked in milk into a paste before it goes in the dough. You'll cook it to 149°F, knead a soft dough to a windowpane, shape four rolls side by side in the pan, and bake to 190°F.

callback.body: Pão de queijo scalds its starch with boiling milk. Tangzhong does the same with a spoonful of flour, so the starch can hold far more water, which keeps the bread moist.

why.title: What tangzhong does
why.body: Starch heated in liquid to about 149°F swells and soaks up several times its weight in water. Mixed into dough, it holds that water through baking, so the loaf is softer, moister, and slower to go stale.

why.title: Bread flour
why.body: Bread flour has more protein than all-purpose, so it builds a stronger gluten net. That net holds a soft, wet dough up tall.

why.title: Four rolls in the pan
why.body: Shaping the dough as four rolled-up pieces stretches the gluten in every direction, so the loaf rises evenly into four domes and pulls apart in layers.

why.title: 190°F inside
why.body: Milk and sugar brown the crust early. The center is set at 190°F.

wrong.fix: It heated too fast. Whisk hard off the heat, or start again on lower heat.
It's meant to be soft. Knead on a lightly oiled counter instead of adding flour.

wrong.sign: The loaf has a big hole under the crust
wrong.fix: It was shaped loosely. Roll each piece up tight.
Tent with foil for the rest of the bake.

quiz.q: What temperature does tangzhong cook to?
What does tangzhong do for the bread?
choices: Holds extra water so it stays soft and fresh longer
quiz.explain: The swollen starch keeps its water.

choices: Its stronger gluten holds up a soft dough

ingredients.text: a little, for the counter and bowl

steps.text: Whisk the tangzhong's flour into its milk in the saucepan. Cook over medium-low heat, whisking, until it reaches 149°F and thickens to a paste.
steps.look: Thick enough that the whisk leaves lines.

steps.text: Scrape it into the large bowl and let it cool to warm.
Stir the warm milk, 1 teaspoon of the sugar, and the yeast in a cup and let it foam.
Add the yeast, the rest of the sugar, the flour, the salt, and the egg to the tangzhong. Mix to a shaggy dough.
Wash your hands, and throw away the shell.
Knead on a lightly oiled counter, working in the butter after 5 minutes, until it passes the windowpane test.
steps.look: Smooth, soft, and stretching thin enough to see light through.

steps.text: Oil the bowl, add the dough, cover, and let it double.
Divide the dough into 4 pieces by weight. Roll each into an 8-by-4-inch oval, fold the long sides into the middle, and roll it up tightly from a short end.
Oil the loaf pan and set the rolls in side by side, seams down. Cover and proof until the dough is 1 inch above the rim. Heat the oven to 350°F for the last half hour.
Brush the top with milk and bake until deep golden.
Check the center from the side: 190°F.
Turn it out onto the rack at once and cool completely before slicing.
steps.tip: Sliced warm, the soft crumb squashes.
